pranayama_sync: Breathe slowly and evenly throughout
ayurvedic_rationale: Halasana folds the body fully inward over the shoulders, producing deep pratyahara and strong stimulation of the thyroid. It is calming and Vata-pacifying when supported, but it loads the cervical spine heavily — the neck must never turn while inverted, and the shoulders, not the neck, carry the weight.

primary_benefits: Builds extreme shoulder stability and back strength
Develops maximal thoracic spinal extension
Sharpens balance, proprioception, and concentration
Opens the entire front line of the body
instructions: Establish a stable, held Forearm Stand against a wall before attempting any backbend.
With the forearms pressing down and the shoulders stacked, begin to lift the head and gaze forward.
Bend the knees and allow the spine to arch, drawing the feet toward the crown of the head.
Keep pressing the forearms down and lifting through the shoulders — the arch must come from the thoracic spine, not a collapsed lower back.
Hold only as long as the shoulders stay engaged and the breath stays even.
Exit by straightening the legs back to vertical, then lowering one leg at a time. Rest in Child's Pose.
pranayama_sync: Even, unforced breath. Any breath-holding means you have gone past your limit.
ayurvedic_rationale: Vrschikasana is one of the most advanced Hatha postures and generates intense heat and Pitta. It is appropriate only for long-established practitioners with unrestricted shoulder and spinal mobility. In an unsupervised setting it should be treated as aspirational rather than prescriptive.

primary_benefits: Calms the brain and helps relieve stress and mild depression
Stimulates the thyroid and prostate glands and abdominal organs
Stretches the shoulders and neck
Tones the legs and buttocks
Improves digestion
Helps relieve the symptoms of menopause
Reduces fatigue and alleviates insomnia
Therapeutic for asthma, infertility, and sinusitis
instructions: From a supine position, the upper back is resting on the earth with the hips straight up towards the sky
The torso is perpendicular to the earth
The legs are fully extended and the toes are active
The hands are either supporting the lower back or extended up by the side body in matchstick
The neck is flat on the earth and the chin is tucked in
The gaze is inward
pranayama_sync: Breathe slowly and evenly throughout
ayurvedic_rationale: Salamba Sarvangasana is called the queen of asanas — sarvanga means all limbs, reflecting its systemic effect. The inversion reverses Apana Vayu and the throat compression regulates the thyroid. It also places substantial load on the cervical spine, so folded blankets under the shoulders are classical practice and the neck is never turned while inverted.

primary_benefits: Builds shoulder, core, and upper-back stability
Improves balance and proprioception
May reduce feelings of fatigue by reversing the usual gravitational load
Encourages focus and calm concentration
instructions: Kneel and place the forearms on the floor with elbows shoulder-width apart.
Interlace the fingers and create a stable cradle for the back of the head.
Place the crown lightly on the floor and lift the knees, walking the feet closer.
Engage the shoulders strongly away from the ears and lift the hips upward.
With control, bring one knee and then the other toward the chest, or lift both legs only if the base is steady.
Keep the neck long and weight primarily in the forearms and shoulders, not the head.
Exit slowly by lowering one leg at a time and resting in Child's Pose or a neutral seated position.
pranayama_sync: Breathe slowly and evenly without strain, using each exhale to stabilize the shoulders and core.
ayurvedic_rationale: Inversion is classically considered highly energizing and can support clarity, especially when kapha or lethargy is prominent. Because it strongly alters pressure and circulation, it must be approached cautiously in pitta- or vata-dominant states and avoided when contraindications are present.

primary_benefits: Mobilises the entire spine through flexion and extension
Warms and lubricates the intervertebral joints before deeper work
Relieves back and neck tension from prolonged sitting
Synchronises breath with movement, settling the mind at the start of practice
instructions: Come to all fours with the wrists directly under the shoulders and the knees under the hips.
Spread the fingers wide and press evenly through the whole hand to protect the wrists.
Inhale into Cow: drop the belly, roll the shoulders back, and lift the tailbone and gaze.
Exhale into Cat: press the floor away, round the spine toward the ceiling, and draw the navel in and the chin toward the chest.
Move one vertebra at a time, letting the breath set the pace rather than the other way round.
Continue for 6 to 10 full rounds, finishing in a neutral spine.
pranayama_sync: Inhale into Cow, exhale into Cat. One full breath per movement.
ayurvedic_rationale: The Cat-Cow pair is the classical spinal warm-up and the safest entry point for every constitution. The rhythmic, breath-linked movement is deeply grounding for Vata, the gentle pace keeps Pitta from rushing into intensity, and the mobilisation breaks up the morning stagnation characteristic of Kapha.

primary_benefits: Builds upper-body and core strength
Improves scapular stability and arm alignment
Conditions the wrists and chest for vinyasa transitions
Develops whole-body control and endurance
instructions: Start in plank with shoulders over wrists and body in one long line.
Shift slightly forward so the shoulders move just ahead of the wrists.
Bend the elbows straight back, keeping them close to the ribs.
Lower until the upper arms are parallel to the floor, avoiding shoulder collapse.
Keep the core and legs active so the hips do not drop or lift too high.
Hold briefly with steady breath, then transition with control or lower to the mat.
pranayama_sync: Exhale as you lower with control and inhale as you stabilize the body in the hover.
ayurvedic_rationale: This heating, effortful pose is useful for reducing Kapha and building agni through disciplined muscular engagement. Because it is strongly activating, it can aggravate Pitta if held too long or practiced with strain.

primary_benefits: Strengthens the entire posterior chain — spinal extensors, glutes, and hamstrings
Builds the postural endurance that protects the lower back
Opens the chest and shoulders
Stimulates the abdominal organs and supports digestive function
instructions: Lie prone with the forehead on the mat, arms alongside the body, palms facing down or up.
Roll the shoulders back and down, drawing the shoulder blades toward one another.
Lengthen the tailbone toward the heels to protect the lumbar spine before lifting anything.
Inhale and lift the head, chest, arms, and legs away from the floor simultaneously.
Reach strongly back through the fingertips and the toes — length first, height second.
Keep the gaze down and slightly forward so the back of the neck stays long. Exhale to lower and rest one cheek on the mat.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lift, hold for a few breaths, exhale to release. Never strain the breath.
ayurvedic_rationale: Salabhasana builds the back-body strength that keeps the spine — the primary seat of Vata — stable and supported. The effort generates warmth, making it valuable for clearing Kapha heaviness. Pitta types should work on length rather than maximum lift, which is where the strain and the heat come from.

primary_benefits: Opens the shoulders and upper back
Stretches the spine without intense load on the wrists
Helps lengthen the lats and armpits
Promotes gentle chest opening and breath expansion
instructions: Begin on hands and knees with hips stacked over knees.
Walk the hands forward while keeping the hips above the knees.
Lower the chest toward the floor and lengthen the tailbone back.
Rest the forehead or chin on the mat if comfortable.
Keep the arms active and broaden across the upper back.
Breathe into the ribs and soften the shoulders away from the ears.
To come out, walk the hands back under the shoulders and sit back on the heels if desired.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to expand the ribs and exhale to soften the chest and shoulders deeper toward the floor.
ayurvedic_rationale: Puppy Pose opens the upper body while keeping the pelvis grounded, which can ease Vata-related tightness in the shoulders and upper back. Its cooling, heart-opening quality can also reduce excess Pitta tension.

primary_benefits: Gently releases tension in the lower back
Encourages passive chest and shoulder opening
Supports relaxation and nervous system downregulation
Helps restore awareness of breath and body position
instructions: Lie face down with your legs extended and the tops of the feet relaxed on the floor.
Turn one cheek to the mat or rest the forehead down if comfortable.
Extend the arms alongside the body with palms facing up or place the hands comfortably by the sides.
Allow the abdomen, ribs, and pelvis to soften into the floor.
Close the eyes and let the breath become slow and even.
Remain still and release effort through the whole body.
To exit, slowly turn the head to center and press up with care.
pranayama_sync: Breathe naturally and let each exhale soften the abdomen and chest into the floor.
ayurvedic_rationale: This quiet prone rest pose is grounding and cooling, helping calm excess Vata and Pitta through stillness and surrender. It is often used to settle the nervous system after more active practice.

primary_benefits: Improves spinal neutrality and postural awareness
Gently strengthens wrists, shoulders, and core
Supports safe preparation for backbends and balance work
Encourages steady breathing and body-mind coordination
instructions: Come onto hands and knees with wrists under shoulders and knees under hips.
Spread the fingers wide and press evenly through the base of the hands.
Lengthen the spine so the back is flat and neutral from tailbone to crown.
Engage the abdomen gently to support the low back.
Keep the neck long and gaze down between the hands.
Breathe steadily and hold without sinking into the shoulders or collapsing the belly.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lengthen the spine and exhale to gently engage the abdomen without rounding the back.
ayurvedic_rationale: This neutral grounding posture helps stabilize excess Vata by creating structure and proprioceptive awareness. Its simple, steady shape also calms the nervous system and prepares the body for more active asana.

primary_benefits: Gently decompresses the lower back and sacrum
Calms the nervous system and lowers heart rate
Releases the hips, thighs, and ankles
Serves as the universal resting position, available at any point in a practice
instructions: Kneel with the big toes touching and the knees either together or as wide as the mat.
Sit the hips back toward the heels; place a folded blanket between the calves and thighs if they do not meet.
Walk the hands forward and lower the forehead to the mat or onto a block or bolster.
Extend the arms forward for a more active shoulder stretch, or rest them alongside the body, palms up, for full surrender.
Let the belly soften completely and breathe into the back of the ribcage.
Stay for at least 8 to 10 slow breaths — this pose works through duration, not effort.
pranayama_sync: Slow diaphragmatic breathing into the back body. Let the exhale be longer than the inhale.
ayurvedic_rationale: Balasana is the posture of return. The forward enclosure and grounding of the forehead settle Vata's restlessness immediately, and the withdrawal of the senses cools Pitta's drive. Kapha types benefit from it as a brief reset rather than an extended stay, which can tip into inertia.

primary_benefits: Neutral spine — completely decompresses all spinal structures
Allows psoas muscle (Vata holding muscle) to fully release
Ideal starting position for yoga nidra or body scan meditation
Lowers cortisol more effectively than seated rest
Safe for almost all injuries and conditions including pregnancy
instructions: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet hip-width apart and flat on the floor.
Let the knees rest against each other — they do not need to be held up.
Rest arms on the belly or out to the sides at 45 degrees, palms up.
Allow the entire weight of the body to release into the floor.
Close eyes. Notice the natural rise and fall of the belly with breath.
Stay 5-15 minutes. This is the safest, most accessible restorative pose.
pranayama_sync: Belly breathing (Diaphragmatic breath) — let the belly rise fully on inhale
ayurvedic_rationale: Vishranti (rest) is the primary medicine for Vata disorders. The constructive rest position allows Prana to redistribute evenly through all channels (Srotas) without effort.

primary_benefits: Calms the brain and helps relieve stress and mild depression
Relaxes the body
Reduces headache, fatigue, and insomnia
Helps to lower blood pressure
instructions: The body rests on the earth in a supine position with the arms resting by the side body
The palms are relaxed and open toward the sky
The shoulder blades are pulled back, down and rolled under comfortably, resting evenly on the earth
The legs are extended down and splayed open
The heels are in and the toes flop out
The eyes are closed
Everything is relaxed
The gaze is inward
pranayama_sync: Slow deep belly breathing throughout
ayurvedic_rationale: Savasana is the most important and least respected posture in the system. It is where the nervous system integrates everything the practice has done — cutting it short discards the benefit of the session. Complete stillness is profoundly Vata-pacifying, and the classical minimum is five minutes, longer for Vata constitutions.

primary_benefits: Deeply calms the nervous system and reduces anxiety
Reverses venous blood flow, reduces leg swelling and fatigue
Lowers cortisol — one of the most effective restorative inversions
Relieves lower back tension and sciatica
Balances Vata and Pitta doshas through passive inversion
instructions: Sit sideways next to a wall with your hip touching it.
Swing your legs up the wall as you lower your back to the floor.
Adjust your distance from the wall so legs are comfortable — slightly bent is fine.
Rest arms out to the sides, palms facing up.
Close eyes and breathe slowly. Let gravity do all the work.
Stay 3-7 minutes. To exit: bend knees, roll to the side, pause, then sit up slowly.
pranayama_sync: 4-7-8 breath: inhale 4 counts, hold 7, exhale 8
ayurvedic_rationale: Viparita Karani is one of the Hatha Yoga Pradipika rejuvenating inversions. It reverses the downward flow of Apana Vata, calms Prana Vata, and cools Pitta. Ideal for evening practice or post-exertion recovery.

primary_benefits: Opens hips and inner groin passively without muscular effort
Stimulates abdominal organs — improves digestion and Agni
Relieves menstrual cramps and menopausal symptoms
Deeply calming — activates parasympathetic nervous system
Balances Vata in the lower body (Apana Kshetra)
instructions: Lie on your back. Bring the soles of the feet together and let knees fall open.
Place a folded blanket or block under each knee if the stretch is too intense.
Rest hands on belly or out to the sides, palms up.
Close eyes, soften the jaw and let the groin completely release.
Breathe deeply into the belly. Hold for 2-6 minutes.
To exit: use hands to press knees together, then hug them to chest.
pranayama_sync: Anulom Vilom — alternate nostril breathing to balance left-right channels
ayurvedic_rationale: Stimulates the Muladhara and Svadhisthana chakras. The passive hip opening releases stored Vata in the lower body. Particularly beneficial after standing or strength practices.

primary_benefits: Deep stretch of quadriceps, hip flexors, and psoas
Improves digestion by stimulating the stomach and intestines
Relieves tired legs after standing all day
Stretches the deep abdominal muscles
Reduces Pitta in the digestive system
instructions: Sit in Hero Pose (Virasana) — kneeling with feet outside hips, sitting between them.
If sitting is painful, place a block or blanket between your feet.
Place hands behind you on the floor and slowly lean back.
Lower to forearms, then (if comfortable) to back. Support lower back with a blanket if needed.
Extend arms overhead or rest them on the belly.
Hold 1-5 minutes. Exit slowly: come back to forearms, then sitting.
pranayama_sync: Breathe into the belly and let each exhale deepen the stretch naturally
ayurvedic_rationale: Supta Virasana stimulates Pachaka Pitta in the stomach region and Samana Vata in the navel. Prescribed in Ashtanga Hridayam for digestive disorders and post-meal heaviness.

primary_benefits: Releases tension along the entire spinal column
Massages abdominal organs — stimulates Agni (digestive fire)
Stretches the IT band, outer hip, and chest
Relieves lower back pain and sacroiliac tension
Wrings out toxins (Ama) from the digestive organs — classical Ayurvedic benefit
instructions: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor.
Draw the right knee to your chest, then cross it over to the left side.
Extend the right arm out at shoulder height, gaze right.
Keep both shoulder blades on the floor. The left hand can rest on the right knee.
Breathe into the right side of the chest. Hold 1-2 minutes each side.
Repeat on the other side.
pranayama_sync: Exhale into the twist on each breath to release deeper
ayurvedic_rationale: Twisting postures are the classical Ayurvedic method to stimulate Samana Vata (digestive wind) and Pachaka Pitta (digestive fire). The supine position makes this accessible even after illness or fatigue.

primary_benefits: Gentle spinal extension without muscular effort
Opens the chest and stimulates the heart and lungs
Calms the nervous system while still energising the body
Relieves lower back fatigue
Balances all three doshas in a single pose
instructions: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet hip-width apart close to the hips.
Press feet firmly into the floor and lift the hips.
Slide a block under the sacrum (not the lumbar spine) at a comfortable height.
Let the block support your weight completely — release all muscular effort.
Arms rest by your sides. Close eyes and breathe into the open chest.
To exit: press feet to lift hips slightly, remove block, lower spine slowly.
pranayama_sync: Chest breathing (Thoracic breath) — let the ribcage expand sideways with each inhale
ayurvedic_rationale: The supported bridge is the safest restorative inversion — it reverses Apana Vata while remaining accessible. Used in Yoga Chikitsa (yogic therapy) for fatigue, insomnia, and mild depression.

primary_benefits: Opens the chest, throat, and front of the body
Counteracts rounded-shoulder posture from desk work
Stimulates thyroid and parathyroid glands
Deepens breathing capacity by expanding the thoracic cavity
Reduces Kapha stagnation in the respiratory system
instructions: Place a yoga block (or rolled blanket) horizontally between your shoulder blades at heart height.
Lie back over the support so the chest opens and the head rests back gently.
Extend legs long, or keep knees bent if lower back is sensitive.
Let arms rest open at your sides, palms facing up.
Allow the chest to expand with each inhale. Hold 2-6 minutes.
To exit: use hands to lift head first, then roll to the side.
pranayama_sync: Ujjayi breath — ocean-sounding breath to fill the expanded chest
ayurvedic_rationale: Opens the Anahata (heart) and Vishuddha (throat) chakras. Clears Kapha from the chest and lungs. Classical Matsyasana is prescribed in Charaka Samhita for respiratory conditions.

primary_benefits: Deeply stretches the entire posterior chain — hamstrings, spine, calves
Stimulates the kidneys and adrenal glands — reduces stress hormones
Calms the mind and relieves mild depression
Improves digestion by compressing the abdominal organs
Pacifies Pitta and Vata through forward folding and surrender
instructions: Sit with legs extended straight ahead. Place a folded blanket under sitting bones if hips are tight.
Rather than forcing the fold, let gravity pull you forward passively.
Rest hands on legs or on a bolster placed over your shins.
Round the spine — this is yin, not yang. Let the back release.
Close eyes, breathe slowly. Hold 2-5 minutes without strain.
Exit slowly — press hands to floor, unroll spine one vertebra at a time.
pranayama_sync: Bhramari (Humming Bee) — hum gently on each exhale to calm the nervous system
ayurvedic_rationale: Paschimottanasana is considered the king of forward folds in classical texts. The passive yin version stimulates kidney health as emphasised in Ashtanga Hridayam for Vata disorders.

primary_benefits: One hour of Yoga Nidra equals 4 hours of sleep for nervous system restoration
Profoundly reduces stress hormones and restores adrenal function
Integrates the physical, emotional, and mental effects of the preceding practice
Balances the autonomic nervous system
Classical Ayurvedic Nidra (sleep) therapy for Vata and Pitta disorders
instructions: Lie in Savasana with eyes closed, a blanket for warmth, and an eye pillow if available.
Set a Sankalpa (intention) — a short positive statement repeated 3 times mentally.
Rotate awareness through each body part from toes to crown — simply notice each part.
Notice any sensations, emotions, or thoughts without reaction. You are the witness.
Follow the natural breath without controlling it.
Stay for 10-20 minutes. Return to waking slowly — wiggle fingers, deepen breath, open eyes.
pranayama_sync: Natural, uncontrolled breath — observe it without changing it
ayurvedic_rationale: Yoga Nidra is the modern systematization of Pratyahara (sense withdrawal) — the 5th limb of Patanjali Ashtanga Yoga. Charaka Samhita prescribes Nidra as one of the three pillars of health alongside Ahara (diet) and Brahmacharya.

primary_benefits: Improves hamstring and hip flexibility
Opens the groins and inner thighs
Builds postural control and core engagement
Supports focus and body awareness
instructions: Sit with both legs extended and lengthen the spine.
Bend the right knee and hold the right big toe or foot with the right hand.
Keep the left leg active and grounded as you draw the right foot toward the side of the face.
Open the right elbow back and lift the chest without collapsing the spine.
Hold the shape with steady breathing, keeping the neck relaxed.
Release slowly and repeat on the other side.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lengthen the spine and exhale as you draw the foot closer, keeping the breath smooth and unforced.
ayurvedic_rationale: This pose is grounding yet energizing, helping to mobilize the hips and legs while sharpening concentration. It is especially useful for reducing Vata’s stiffness and Kapha’s heaviness through directed effort and opening.

primary_benefits: Opens the hips, groin, and inner thighs
Stimulates circulation to the pelvis and abdominal organs
Relieves menstrual discomfort and supports reproductive health
Grounds and settles the nervous system through a stable seated base
instructions: Sit on the front edge of a folded blanket with the legs extended.
Bend both knees and bring the soles of the feet together, drawing the heels toward the pelvis.
Hold the feet or the ankles and let the knees release toward the floor under their own weight.
Support the outer thighs with blocks or cushions if the knees sit high — hanging unsupported strains the medial knee.
Lengthen the spine on an inhale, crown lifting; on an exhale, fold forward from the hips if comfortable.
Hold for 1 to 3 minutes, breathing into the groin and inner thighs.
pranayama_sync: Slow, even breathing. Direct the exhale into the inner thighs to invite release.
ayurvedic_rationale: Baddha Konasana works directly on the pelvic floor and the Apana Vayu that governs elimination and reproduction — the primary seat of Vata. Classically prescribed for menstrual and prostate health. The grounded base and open hips make it one of the most reliably Vata-pacifying seated postures.

primary_benefits: Deeply opens the outer hips, glutes, and piriformis
Stretches the shoulders, triceps, and chest in opposing rotations
Reveals and helps correct left-right asymmetry
Improves posture by opening the front of the shoulder
instructions: From a seated position, bend the right knee and place the right foot outside the left hip.
Cross the left knee over the right, stacking the knees, and bring the left foot outside the right hip.
Sit on a folded blanket so the pelvis stays level; if the top knee floats high, sit higher.
Reach the left arm up, bend the elbow, and let the left hand drop down the spine.
Reach the right arm out to the side, rotate it inward, and bend the elbow to bring the right hand up the back — clasp the fingers or hold a strap between them.
Lift the chest and keep the head neutral. Hold, then unwind and reverse both the legs and the arms.
pranayama_sync: Steady breathing. Exhale into the outer hip and the shoulder simultaneously.
ayurvedic_rationale: Gomukhasana releases the outer hips and shoulders where Vata's tension characteristically accumulates. Its pronounced left-right asymmetry makes it diagnostic — the tighter side reveals where the body compensates. The strap is not a lesser version; forcing the clasp is what injures the rotator cuff.

primary_benefits: Establishes the stable seated base for pranayama and meditation
Gently opens the hips and lengthens the spine
Calms the mind and slows the breath
Builds the postural endurance needed for sustained sitting
instructions: Sit on the front edge of a folded blanket or cushion so the hips are higher than the knees.
Cross the shins comfortably, letting each foot rest under the opposite knee.
Let the knees release toward the floor; support them with cushions if they sit high.
Stack the head over the heart and the heart over the pelvis, lengthening the spine without rigidity.
Rest the hands on the knees or in the lap, palms up to receive or down to ground.
Soften the jaw, the eyes, and the shoulders. Change the cross of the legs halfway through.
pranayama_sync: The seat for all pranayama. Let the breath settle to its natural rhythm before beginning any technique.
ayurvedic_rationale: Sukhasana means the comfortable seat — sukha, ease. It is the foundational asana for pranayama and dhyana. The grounded base and symmetrical stillness pacify Vata directly, which is why every classical text places it at the start of the subtle practices.

primary_benefits: Intensely opens the outer hips, glutes, and piriformis
Relieves sciatic-type referral from piriformis tightness
Improves external rotation of the hip joint
Releases the deep pelvic holding built up by prolonged sitting
instructions: Sit on a folded blanket with the legs extended, then bend the left knee and place the left shin on the floor parallel to the front edge of the mat.
Stack the right shin directly on top of the left, right ankle over left knee and right knee over left ankle.
If the top knee floats, fill the gap with a folded blanket rather than pressing the knee down.
Flex both feet strongly to protect the knee ligaments — this is not optional in this pose.
Sit tall on an inhale; on an exhale, walk the hands forward and fold from the hips.
Hold for up to 2 minutes, then switch the stack of the legs.
pranayama_sync: Long, slow exhales into the outer hip. Resist the urge to hold the breath against the intensity.
ayurvedic_rationale: Agnistambhasana means fire log — the stacked shins resemble logs laid for a fire, and the pose kindles the pelvic Agni. The deep hip release addresses the Apana Vayu region where Vata lodges most stubbornly. Both feet must stay flexed; a passive foot transfers the load straight into the medial knee.

primary_benefits: Opens the hips and glutes deeply
Releases tension in the outer hip and lower back
Improves mobility in the hip joint
Supports emotional release and relaxation
instructions: From Downward-Facing Dog or Tabletop, bring one knee forward behind the wrist.
Angle the front shin comfortably on the mat and extend the back leg straight behind you.
Square the hips toward the front of the mat as much as possible without strain.
Inhale to lengthen the spine, then exhale to fold forward over the front leg if appropriate.
Rest the forearms or forehead on the floor or a prop for support.
Hold with slow breathing, then press back and repeat on the other side.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to create length in the spine and exhale to soften the hips, allowing the breath to deepen the release without forcing the fold.
ayurvedic_rationale: This hip opener helps mobilize apana vata and release accumulated tension in the pelvis and lower back. Its grounding, lengthening quality can be calming for vata and pitta when practiced gently with support.

primary_benefits: Stretches the quadriceps, ankles, and tops of the feet
Provides an alternative meditation seat for tight hips
Classically practised after eating to aid digestion
Improves ankle mobility and relieves plantar tension
instructions: Kneel with the knees together and the feet slightly wider than the hips, tops of the feet flat on the floor.
Place a block or bolster between the feet and sit down onto it — sitting directly on the heels compresses the knee.
Point the toes straight back and press the tops of the feet down evenly.
Rest the hands on the thighs and lengthen the spine, lifting the crown.
Broaden the collarbones and let the shoulder blades settle down the back.
Begin with 1 minute and build gradually; come out slowly and extend the legs if the feet go numb.
pranayama_sync: A stable seat for pranayama. Keep the spine long so the diaphragm moves freely.
ayurvedic_rationale: Virasana is the hero's seat, valued as a pranayama posture where crossed-leg sitting is inaccessible. Vajrasana and Virasana are the two asanas traditionally permitted after a meal, as the position directs circulation toward the digestive organs and kindles Agni. Props here are classical practice, not modern compromise.

primary_benefits: Deeply stretches the hamstrings
Improves hip flexion and mobility
Strengthens the core and postural muscles
Develops balance, patience, and concentration
instructions: Sit tall with both legs extended forward.
Bend the right knee and bring the foot close to the sitting bone.
Hold the right foot or ankle with both hands and lengthen the spine.
Slowly extend the right leg upward without rounding the back.
Keep the left leg active and the shoulders relaxed away from the ears.
Hold with steady breath, then lower with control and repeat on the other side.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lengthen through the spine and exhale as you extend the leg, avoiding any jerking or breath-holding.
ayurvedic_rationale: This pose creates strong directional energy and can help counter Kapha’s heaviness through effortful extension. Because it is intense on the hamstrings, it should be approached carefully to avoid aggravating Vata if the body is already dry or tight.

primary_benefits: Supports meditation and breath awareness
Encourages hip external rotation and opening
Promotes a stable, upright seated posture
Calms the mind and supports introspection
instructions: Sit on the floor or a folded blanket with the spine tall.
Bend one knee and place that foot high on the opposite thigh if the hip allows.
Bend the other knee and place the second foot on the opposite thigh.
Keep both knees moving downward without forcing them toward the floor.
Rest the hands on the knees or in a meditation mudra and lengthen the spine.
Breathe steadily and remain relaxed; come out slowly and switch sides if practicing asymmetrically.
pranayama_sync: Breathe slowly and evenly, allowing each exhale to soften the hips and settle the mind.
ayurvedic_rationale: Padmasana is a classic meditative seat that promotes steadiness, inward focus, and pranic containment. It is considered especially supportive for calming vata and cultivating sattvic clarity when the joints can safely accommodate the position.

primary_benefits: Lengthens the spine and creates space between the vertebrae
Opens the shoulders, lats, and the side body
Expands the ribcage and improves breathing capacity
Corrects the thoracic rounding of desk posture from a stable seated base
instructions: Sit in a stable cross-legged position or in Virasana on a folded blanket.
Interlace the fingers and turn the palms to face away from you.
Inhale and extend the arms straight overhead, palms pressing toward the ceiling.
Draw the lower ribs in so the lift comes from the thoracic spine rather than an arching lower back.
Keep the shoulders drawing away from the ears and the biceps alongside them.
Hold for 5 to 8 breaths, then release and change the interlace of the fingers.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lift and lengthen, exhale to settle the shoulders down.
ayurvedic_rationale: Parvatasana is the seated mountain — steady, grounded, and rising. The overhead extension lifts the Kapha heaviness that settles in the chest and upper back, while the stable seat keeps the practice grounding rather than agitating for Vata.

primary_benefits: Establishes the neutral pelvis and long spine that every seated pose is built on
Strengthens the deep postural muscles of the back
Stretches the hamstrings and calves actively
Builds the awareness needed to fold safely from the hips
instructions: Sit with the legs extended straight in front, feet hip-width apart and strongly flexed.
Sit on a folded blanket if the lower back rounds — the pelvis must be neutral, not tipped back.
Press the backs of the thighs down and engage the quadriceps so the kneecaps draw up.
Place the palms flat beside the hips, fingers pointing forward, and press down to lift the sternum.
Stack the shoulders over the hips and the ears over the shoulders.
Hold for 5 to 10 breaths, maintaining the length of the spine throughout.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lengthen the spine, exhale to root the sitting bones down.
ayurvedic_rationale: Dandasana is the staff — a straight, upright axis. It is to seated postures what Tadasana is to standing: the reference alignment against which everything else is measured. The active engagement steadies Vata, and the upright axis prevents the collapse into Kapha heaviness.

primary_benefits: Improves digestion and supports post-meal comfort
Promotes grounded posture and pelvic stability
Helps calm the nervous system and reduce mental restlessness
Encourages ankle, knee, and toe mobility
instructions: Kneel on the floor with your big toes touching and your knees together or comfortably apart.
Sit back onto your heels, keeping the tops of the feet flat on the floor.
Lengthen your spine and rest your hands on your thighs.
Relax the shoulders and soften the belly while keeping the chest open.
Close the eyes or gaze softly forward and breathe steadily.
To come out, lift the hips off the heels and extend the legs slowly.
pranayama_sync: Breathe slowly through the nose, allowing each exhale to lengthen and settle the body into stillness.
ayurvedic_rationale: Vajrasana is traditionally used after eating because it supports agni without adding strain or excess movement. Its steady, grounded shape helps pacify vata and pitta while encouraging mindful digestion and quiet awareness.

primary_benefits: Strengthens the abdomen, hip flexors, and spine
Stimulates the kidneys, thyroid and prostate glands, and intestines
Helps relieve stress
Improves digestion
instructions: From a seated position the feet are lifted up so that the thighs are angled about 45-50 degrees relative to the earth
The tailbone is lengthened into the earth and the pubis pulls toward the navel
The shoulder blades are spread across the back and the hands reach around the back of the calves, with legs pulled towards the body
The chin is tipped slightly toward the sternum so that the base of the skull lifts lightly away from the back of the neck
Gaze is forward
pranayama_sync: Inhale to ground, exhale to stabilize
ayurvedic_rationale: Navasana kindles Agni directly through sustained abdominal contraction, and the classical texts prescribe it for sluggish digestion and Ama accumulation. The heat and effort strongly reduce Kapha. Bend the knees rather than rounding the lower back — a collapsed lumbar spine turns a digestive pose into a back injury.

primary_benefits: Relieves the spine and neck
Energizes the body
instructions: From box neutral shift some weight to the palms
The wrists, elbows and shoulders are in one line
The abdomen is pulled in and up with the spine arched in a strong Cobra spine
The crown of the head is towards the earth and the neck is relaxed
The gaze is between the arms towards the belly
pranayama_sync: Inhale to ground, exhale to stabilize
ayurvedic_rationale: Marjaryasana is the flexion half of the Cat-Cow pair, drawing the navel in and rounding the spine. The breath-linked movement is the classical spinal warm-up and among the safest postures for every constitution — grounding for Vata, unhurried for Pitta, and mobilising for the stagnation of Kapha.

primary_benefits: Strengthens the ankles, thighs, calves, and spine
Stretches shoulders and chest
Stimulates the abdominal organs, diaphragm, and heart
Reduces flat feet
Energizes the entire body
instructions: From a standing position, the feet are together and rooted into the earth with toes actively lifted
The knees are bent and the weight of the body is on the heels of the feet
The pelvis is tucked in and the ribcage is lifted
The neck is a natural extension of the spine
The arms are lifted up toward the sky with the elbows straight and the biceps by the ears
The hands can be together or separated and facing each other with the fingers spread wide
The gaze is forward
pranayama_sync: Inhale to ground, exhale to stabilize
ayurvedic_rationale: Utkatasana means fierce or powerful, and the sustained effort generates heat quickly. It is strongly Kapha-reducing and builds the leg strength that supports every standing posture. Pitta types should resist making it a contest of endurance; the pose is complete when the knees start tracking inward, not when the thighs give out.

primary_benefits: Stretches the rib cage, arms and torso
Tones the oblique muscles
instructions: From mountain pose, on the inhalation bring the hands up and interlace the fingers together
Exhale, bend to one side, lengthening the opposite of the rib cage and stretch
pranayama_sync: Inhale to ground, exhale to stabilize
ayurvedic_rationale: Alanasana opens the hip flexors and psoas of the back leg while the upward reach expands the chest. The lifted, expansive shape counters Kapha heaviness, and the strong grounding of the front foot steadies Vata. Keep the tailbone lengthening down so the extension stays in the upper back.

primary_benefits: Calms the brain and helps relieve stress and mild depression
Energizes the body
Stretches the shoulders, neck, hamstrings, calves, arches, and hands
Strengthens the arms and legs
Helps relieve the symptoms of menopause
Relieves menstrual discomfort when done with the head supported
Helps prevent osteoporosis
Improves digestion
Relieves headache, insomnia, back pain, and fatigue
Therapeutic for high blood pressure, asthma, flat feet, sciatica, and sinusitis
instructions: From downward_dog
html the legs are straight with the sits bones tilted up and reaching for the sky
The feet are flat with the heels firmly rooted
One palm is flat with the knuckles evenly pressed into the earth
The other hand reaches under the body and grasps the opposite ankle
The spine is long and the heart is open toward the sky
The neck is loose and the crown of the head is relaxed toward the earth
The gaze is toward the center
pranayama_sync: Inhale to ground, exhale to stabilize
ayurvedic_rationale: Adho Mukha Svanasana is the resting and transitional posture of the whole Hatha system, and a mild inversion in its own right. The head-below-heart position cools Pitta and calms the mind, while the full-body engagement clears Kapha. Bend the knees freely — length in the spine is the point, not straight legs.

primary_benefits: Opens the hip flexors and psoas of the back leg
Stretches the groin and strengthens the front thigh
Improves hip mobility restricted by prolonged sitting
Serves as the transitional posture of the Surya Namaskar sequence
instructions: From a standing forward fold, step the right foot back and lower the right knee to the mat.
Position the left knee directly over the left ankle — never let it travel past the toes.
Place the fingertips on the floor either side of the front foot, or on blocks to bring the floor up.
Inhale and lift the chest, drawing the shoulder blades down and lengthening the front of the right hip.
Tuck the tailbone slightly to protect the lower back and deepen the hip flexor stretch.
Gaze forward. Hold for 3 to 5 breaths, then change sides.
pranayama_sync: Inhale as you step back and lift the chest.
ayurvedic_rationale: Ashwa Sanchalanasana is steps 4 and 9 of Surya Namaskar. The deep hip flexor opening releases the psoas, which classically holds the physical residue of stress and where Vata's tension lodges. The forward, upward gaze lifts Kapha's inertia.

primary_benefits: Strengthens and stretches the legs, knees, and ankles
Stretches the groin, spine, waist, chest, lungs, and shoulders
Stimulates abdominal organs
Increases stamina
instructions: From warrior II the lower body stays static while the upper body is folded forward at the crease of the hip
One arm is extended toward the front with the bicep by the ear and the fingers spread wide while the other reaches down to the earth on the inside of the thigh
The upper torso and the gaze twist up towards the sky
pranayama_sync: Inhale to ground, exhale to stabilize
ayurvedic_rationale: Utthita Parsvakonasana creates one long line from the back heel to the top fingertips, opening the entire side body and the intercostals — expanding the field of Prana Vayu. The strong legs ground Vata while the lateral opening keeps Kapha from settling in the ribcage.

primary_benefits: Stretches the ankles, groins and back torso
Tones the belly
instructions: From a squatting position the feet are as close together as possible (keep your heels on the floor if you can; otherwise, support them on a folded mat)
The thighs are slightly wider than the torso
The torso is leaning gently forward and tucked snugly between the thighs
The elbows are pressed against the inner knees and the palms are together in Anjali Mudra (Salutation Seal)
The knees resist the elbows to help lengthen the front torso
The gaze is soft and forward
pranayama_sync: Inhale to ground, exhale to stabilize
ayurvedic_rationale: Malasana is the natural resting squat, and it works directly on Apana Vayu — the downward-moving air governing elimination. Classically prescribed for constipation and pelvic stagnation, and valuable in pregnancy preparation. A rolled blanket under the heels is standard where the ankles do not yet allow the squat.

primary_benefits: Opens the side body and intercostal muscles
Improves spinal lateral flexibility
Stretches hamstrings, hips, and shoulders
Encourages deeper breathing into the rib cage
instructions: Kneel upright with the right leg extended out to the side and the left knee under the left hip.
Turn the right foot so the toes point forward or slightly up, keeping the left thigh vertical.
Inhale and extend both arms out to the sides at shoulder height.
Exhale and reach the right hand toward the right leg while the left arm arcs overhead.
Lengthen through both sides of the waist without collapsing into the lower back.
Hold the pose with steady breaths, then return to center and repeat on the other side.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to create length through the spine and side body, then exhale as you deepen the lateral bend without strain.
ayurvedic_rationale: Parighasana opens channels of prana through the ribs and flanks, helping release stagnation and improve breath flow. It is especially useful for balancing kapha heaviness and vata tightness while gently stimulating circulation.

primary_benefits: Strengthens the thighs, glutes, and hips
Opens the inner thighs and groin
Builds lower-body endurance
Encourages grounding and confidence
instructions: Stand with feet wider than hip-width and turn the toes out slightly.
Bend the knees and lower the hips into a wide squat, keeping the knees tracking over the toes.
Stack the knees roughly over the ankles and keep the pelvis neutral.
Lengthen the spine and lift the chest without overarching the low back.
Bring the arms into cactus or shoulder-height bend, or keep hands at the heart.
Press evenly through all four corners of each foot and hold the posture with steady breath.
To come out, straighten the legs slowly and return to standing.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lift the chest and exhale to sink the hips a little lower while keeping the breath steady and unstrained.
ayurvedic_rationale: Goddess Pose is grounding and strengthening, often used to increase stable agni without overheating the system. The wide, rooted stance can support kapha by promoting activation while helping vata feel contained and supported.

primary_benefits: Strengthens the abdomen, hip flexors and spine
Stimulates the kidneys, thyroid, prostate glands and intestines
Helps relieve stress
Improves digestion
instructions: From a seated position the hands are gripped around the back of the legs and the knees are bent in a 90 degree angle
Both legs are pulled in towards the abdomen
The core is engaged to maintain balance on the sits bones (be sure that the back does not round)
The front of the torso lengthens between the pubis and top of the sternum as the spine extends in both directions reaching up to the sky and rooting down to the earth
The gaze is forward and Bandhas are engaged
pranayama_sync: Inhale to ground, exhale to stabilize
ayurvedic_rationale: Ardha Navasana is the accessible entry to Navasana, with the shins parallel to the floor so the lower back stays supported. It kindles Agni through abdominal engagement while asking far less of the hip flexors, making it the correct starting point for anyone whose lumbar spine rounds in the full pose.

primary_benefits: Strengthens the legs, glutes, and core
Improves balance and coordination
Opens the hip flexors and chest
Builds stamina and dynamic stability
instructions: From a standing fold or Downward-Facing Dog, step one foot forward between the hands.
Lift the back heel and straighten the back leg with the toes angled slightly forward.
Bend the front knee to stack it over the ankle and engage the thighs.
Lift the torso and arms overhead or keep hands at the hips for balance.
Square the hips as much as possible and lengthen through the spine.
Hold with steady breath, then step back and repeat on the other side.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to rise and expand through the chest, and exhale to stabilize the legs and core while keeping the breath smooth.
ayurvedic_rationale: This pose creates heat, stability, and forward-moving energy, making it useful for reducing kapha sluggishness and strengthening agni. Its grounding structure can support vata when practiced with measured breath and alignment.

primary_benefits: Stretches the thighs, groins (psoas), abdomen, chest, shoulders and neck
Stimulates the abdominal organs
Opens the shoulders and chest
instructions: From a seated position with the hips squared, one leg is extended forward with the knee bent and parallel to the earth
The front heel is rooted close to the groin (or extended out in a 90 degree angle if flexibility allows)
The other leg is extended back with the knee bent and perpendicular to the earth
The back foot is hooked on the inside of the elbow of the back arm
The front elbow is bent upward perpendicular to the earth with the bicep by the ear
The fingers are interlaced to connect the bind behind the body and assist in opening the chest
The gaze is natural and forward
pranayama_sync: Inhale to ground, exhale to stabilize
ayurvedic_rationale: Eka Pada Rajakapotasana combines a deep hip opening with a full backbend — the hips release Apana Vayu while the chest opening awakens Prana Vayu. It is demanding and heating, best suited to Kapha constitutions, and requires the hips to be genuinely open first; forcing the backbend to compensate for tight hips is what injures the lower back.

primary_benefits: Deeply opens the hip flexors, hamstrings, and inner groin
Releases the psoas and the deep external rotators
Improves hip mobility for squatting and lunging
Relieves lower back tension caused by tight hip flexors
instructions: From Downward-Facing Dog, step the right foot to the outside of the right hand.
Lower the left knee to the mat, or keep the back leg lifted and strong for more intensity.
Walk the right foot slightly further right and turn the toes out about 45 degrees.
Stay on the hands, or lower to the forearms — onto blocks first if the floor is far away.
Let the right hip sink and keep the chest broad rather than collapsing between the shoulders.
Hold for 5 to 10 slow breaths, then press back to Downward Dog and change sides.
pranayama_sync: Long, slow breaths. Let each exhale invite the hip to descend a little further.
ayurvedic_rationale: Utthan Pristhasana works the pelvic region governed by Apana Vayu, releasing the stagnation that accumulates from sedentary living. The long hold suits a Yin approach and is deeply Vata-pacifying when supported on forearms or blocks — unsupported, at depth, it becomes Vata-aggravating.

primary_benefits: Stretches the hip flexors and quadriceps
Improves balance and lower-body mobility
Opens the chest and supports upright posture
Gently energizes the body and improves circulation
instructions: Step one foot forward between the hands and lower the back knee to the mat.
Align the front knee over the ankle and keep the back toes tucked or the top of the foot down.
Lift the torso upright and draw the hips gently forward and down.
Reach the arms overhead or keep the hands on the front thigh for support.
Lengthen through the spine while keeping the lower ribs soft.
Breathe evenly, then release the pose and switch sides.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lift the chest and lengthen the spine, and exhale to soften the hips and deepen the stretch without collapsing.
ayurvedic_rationale: This gentle lunge opens the front body and hips, helping move stagnant kapha and restore healthy circulation. Its steady, grounding quality can soothe vata while building warmth without excessive intensity.

primary_benefits: Establishes the alignment blueprint that every standing pose inherits
Builds postural awareness and improves everyday standing habits
Strengthens the feet, ankles, and legs
Grounds and centres the mind at the start of practice
instructions: Stand with the feet either together or hip-width apart, whichever is steadier.
Root down through all four corners of each foot — big toe mound, little toe mound, and both sides of the heel.
Lift the arches, engage the quadriceps, and let the kneecaps draw up without locking the knees.
Find a neutral pelvis: neither tucked under nor tipped forward.
Lengthen the spine, broaden the collarbones, and let the arms hang with the palms facing forward.
Stack the crown over the pelvis and soften the face. Stand for 5 to 10 breaths, feeling the body settle.
pranayama_sync: Natural, unforced breathing. Feel the breath move the whole body subtly.
ayurvedic_rationale: Tadasana is the mountain — immovable, rooted, quietly alert. It is the single most Vata-pacifying posture in the system, because it asks for nothing but presence and grounding. Every practice should begin here, establishing the connection to the earth element before movement starts.

primary_benefits: Calms the brain
Stretches the spine, the shoulders, the hips and the hamstrings
Strengthens the legs
Stimulates the abdominal organs
Improves posture and sense of balance
Improves digestion
instructions: From a standing position with one leg forward and one back lean the torso forward at the crease of the hip joint
Stop when the torso is parallel to the floor
Press the fingertips or flat palms to the floor on either side of the front foot, maintaining a straight elongated spine
If it isn’t possible to touch the floor, or to maintain a straight spine, support the hands on a pair of blocks
Press the thighs back and lengthen the torso forward, lifting up through the top of the sternum
Then, as flexibility allows, bring the front torso closer to the top of the thigh without rounding the spine
Eventually the long front torso will rest down on the thigh
The gaze is down
pranayama_sync: Inhale to ground, exhale to stabilize
ayurvedic_rationale: Parsvottanasana is an intense one-sided forward fold over a straight front leg, cooling and inward in character and therefore Pitta-pacifying. The narrow stance makes it a genuine balance challenge. Blocks under the hands are standard — rounding the spine to reach the floor defeats the purpose of the pose.

primary_benefits: Strengthens and stretches the legs, knees, and ankles
Stretches the groin, spine, waist, chest, lungs, and shoulders
Stimulates abdominal organs
Increases stamina
Relieves backaches, especially through second trimester of pregnancy
Therapeutic for carpal tunnel syndrome, flat feet, infertility, osteoporosis, and sciatica
instructions: From warrior II , the lower body stays static while the upper body arches back in a gentle back bend
The top arm is extended back with the bicep by the ear and the fingers spread wide
The other arm slides down the back leg resting on the thigh or shin, but not the knee joint
The gaze is up towards the sky
pranayama_sync: Inhale to ground, exhale to stabilize
ayurvedic_rationale: Parsva Virabhadrasana opens the side body from a strong warrior base, lengthening the intercostals and expanding breathing capacity. The combination of grounded legs and expansive upper body is balancing for Vata, while the lateral opening clears the Kapha that settles across the ribs. Keep the weight in the legs rather than collapsing into the lower back.

primary_benefits: Opens the hips and inner thighs
Strengthens the legs and glutes
Improves balance and mobility in the ankles
Builds functional lower-body strength and agility
instructions: Start in a wide-legged stance with the feet turned slightly outward.
Shift your weight into one bent knee while keeping the other leg extended.
Sit the hips back and down as far as comfortable, keeping the chest lifted.
Place the hands on the floor, at the heart, or on the bent thigh for support.
Keep the extended foot active and the heel grounded or lifted as appropriate.
Hold the position with steady breath, then transfer to the other side.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lengthen through the spine and exhale as you sink into the side lunge, maintaining smooth, grounded breathing.
ayurvedic_rationale: Skandasana is mobilizing and strengthening, making it useful for reducing Kapha stagnation while building stable heat in the legs. Its wide, grounded shape also supports Vata by encouraging steadiness and lower-body containment.

primary_benefits: Stretches the insides and backs of the legs
Stimulates the abdominal organs
Strengthens the spine
Calms the brain
Releases groin
instructions: From a wide stance the legs are open and extended sideways to your degree of flexibility
The outer edges of the feet are rotated and gripping toward the earth
The weight of the body is supported by the arms
The palms are rooted into the earth with the fingers pointing towards the body
There should be no excess weight on the knee or ankle joints as you lower down to your degree of flexibility
The gaze is down and slightly forward
pranayama_sync: Inhale to ground, exhale to stabilize
ayurvedic_rationale: Upavistha Konasana is a wide-angle seated forward fold that opens the adductors and hamstrings while the forward orientation cools and calms. Classically valuable for pelvic circulation and reproductive health. Sit elevated on a blanket and fold from the hips — rounding from the waist puts the load straight into the lumbar discs.

primary_benefits: Stretches and strengthens the thighs, knees, and ankles
Stretches the hips, groin, hamstrings, calves, shoulders, chest, and spine
Stimulates the abdominal organs
Helps relieve stress
Improves digestion
Helps relieve the symptoms of menopause
Relieves backache, especially through second trimester of pregnancy
Therapeutic for anxiety, flat feet, infertility, neck pain, osteoporosis, and sciatica
instructions: From a standing position, the legs are straight and separated into a wide stance
The feet are aligned and flat on the earth with the back foot in a 60-degree angle towards the front
The inner thighs are rotated externally away from each other
The pelvis is tucked and the ribcage is lifted
One arm extends up towards the sky as the other reaches down to the earth
Both arms are aligned with the shoulders in a straight line
The fingers reach out as the shoulder blades squeeze together
The gaze is toward the front
pranayama_sync: Inhale to ground, exhale to stabilize
ayurvedic_rationale: Trikonasana is the archetypal standing posture, creating stable triangles through the legs and torso. The strong grounding through both feet is markedly Vata-pacifying, while the side-body opening and spinal length keep Kapha from settling. Reach for the shin or a block rather than the floor — the length of the side body matters more than the depth of the reach.

primary_benefits: Lengthens the whole side body, spine, and shoulders
Expands the ribcage and increases breathing capacity
Improves posture by opening the front of the shoulders
Energises the body as the second step of Surya Namaskar
instructions: Begin in Tadasana with the feet rooted and the legs engaged.
Inhale and sweep the arms out to the sides and overhead in a wide arc.
Bring the palms together overhead, or keep them shoulder-width apart if the shoulders are tight.
Draw the lower ribs in and lengthen the tailbone down so the lift comes from the upper back.
Roll the shoulders away from the ears; keep the biceps beside them.
Gaze forward or softly up at the thumbs. Exhale to release the arms down with control.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to sweep the arms up, exhale to lower.
ayurvedic_rationale: Urdhva Hastasana is step 2 of Surya Namaskar — the upward salute to the sun. The expansive overhead reach lifts Kapha heaviness and awakens Prana Vayu in the chest. Those with high blood pressure or shoulder restriction should keep the arms parallel rather than pressing the palms together.

primary_benefits: Stretches the chest, lungs, shoulders, neck, belly and groin (psoas)
Strengthens the shoulders, arms and back muscles
Strengthens and stretches the thighs, calves and ankles
instructions: From a standing position, the legs are in a wide stance with the feet aligned and flat on the earth
The back foot is in a 60-degree angle towards the front
The hips are squared
The inner thighs are rotated towards each other
The front knee is bent in a 90-degree angle directly above the ankle
The arms extend up to the sky with the biceps by the ears
The hands can be together or separated and facing each other with the fingers spread wide
The ribcage is lifted and the pelvis tucked
The gaze is forward
pranayama_sync: Inhale to ground, exhale to stabilize
ayurvedic_rationale: Virabhadrasana One faces forward and reaches up, building determination and heat. Strongly Kapha-reducing and grounding for Vata through the powerful leg engagement. Pitta types should soften the jaw and gaze — the pose invites a striving quality that quickly tips into aggravation.

primary_benefits: Strengthens and stretches the legs and ankles
Stretches the groin, chest, lungs, and shoulders
Stimulates abdominal organs
