Therapeutic for carpal tunnel syndrome, flat feet, infertility, osteoporosis, and sciatica
instructions: From a standing position, the legs are separated into a wide stance
The front knee is bent in a 90-degree angle directly above the ankle
The back leg is extended and straight with the outside edge of the back foot gripping the earth in a 60-degree angle towards the front
The inner thighs are externally rotated away from each other
The pelvis is tucked
The ribcage is lifted
The arms are extended out to the sides and are aligned with the shoulders in a straight line with the fingers reaching out as the shoulder blades squeeze together
The gaze is toward the front fingers
pranayama_sync: Inhale to ground, exhale to stabilize
ayurvedic_rationale: Virabhadrasana Two opens laterally into a wide, stable base with the gaze steady over the front hand. The broad grounding is deeply Vata-pacifying and the sustained hold generates the heat that clears Kapha. The classical instruction is to hold the gaze soft while the legs work hard — strength without strain.

primary_benefits: Creates a gentle side-body stretch from ankles to fingertips
Opens the hips and outer thighs
Releases tension in the waist, ribs, and shoulders
Supports relaxation and parasympathetic recovery
instructions: Lie on your back and shift your hips slightly to one side of the mat.
Walk both feet and then both arms to the same side, creating a crescent shape.
Keep the shoulders and pelvis grounded as much as possible.
Cross the outside ankle over the inside ankle if that feels comfortable, or keep the legs parallel.
Breathe into the stretched side body and soften the jaw and belly.
To exit, uncross the legs if needed and return the arms and feet to center before repeating on the other side.
pranayama_sync: Breathe slowly into the open side ribs, using each exhale to soften the waist and outer hip.
ayurvedic_rationale: This passive side bend creates space through the lateral channels of the body, helping release accumulated tension without overheating the system. It is soothing for vata and pitta while gently unwinding muscular tightness after more active practice.

primary_benefits: Strengthens the glutes, hamstrings, and spinal extensors
Opens the chest, shoulders, and hip flexors
Stimulates the thyroid through gentle throat compression
Relieves lower back pain by strengthening the posterior chain
instructions: Lie supine with the knees bent, feet flat and hip-width apart, heels close enough to graze with the fingertips.
Keep the feet parallel and the knees tracking directly over the ankles throughout.
Press the feet and the arms down, and lift the hips by peeling the spine off the floor one vertebra at a time.
Roll the shoulders underneath and either interlace the fingers beneath you or hold the edges of the mat.
Keep the glutes active but not gripping, and the chin slightly away from the chest — never turn the head while lifted.
Hold for 5 to 8 breaths, then lower slowly, vertebra by vertebra, and let the knees knock together to release.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lift the hips, exhale to lower. Breathe into the chest while held.
ayurvedic_rationale: Setu Bandha means bridge formation, and the pose builds exactly that — a supported span across the front body. It is gently heating and Kapha-reducing while remaining accessible to Vata thanks to the floor contact throughout. The supported variation on a block is one of the most restorative postures available.

primary_benefits: Opens the hips and inner groins
Relieves tension in the lower back and sacrum
Encourages gentle spinal decompression
Promotes relaxation and playful release
instructions: Lie on your back and draw both knees toward your chest.
Hold the outer edges of the feet, ankles, or shins.
Open the knees wider than the torso while keeping the low back relaxed on the floor.
Stack each ankle over the knee so the shins are roughly vertical.
Gently press the feet into the hands while the tailbone stays heavy.
Breathe evenly, then release the feet and lower the legs back down slowly.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to widen the back body and exhale to soften the hips, keeping the breath smooth and unforced.
ayurvedic_rationale: Ananda Balasana helps release stored tension in the hips and lower back, areas where vata commonly accumulates. Its light, playful quality can also reduce excess pitta rigidity and support a calm, settled state.

primary_benefits: Releases and decompresses the lower back
Compresses and stimulates the ascending and descending colon, relieving trapped wind
Gently stretches the glutes and lower spine
Calms the nervous system and settles the abdomen
instructions: Lie supine with the legs extended and the whole spine settled on the mat.
Exhale and draw both knees in toward the chest.
Wrap the arms around the shins, or hold behind the thighs if the knees are sensitive.
Let the lower back release and widen against the floor; keep the tailbone heavy.
Keep the head and shoulders resting down — there is no need to lift the chin toward the knees.
Optionally rock gently side to side to massage the lumbar spine. Hold for 8 to 10 breaths.
pranayama_sync: Exhale to draw the knees in, inhale to let them float slightly away. Move with the breath.
ayurvedic_rationale: Apanasana is named directly for Apana Vayu, the downward-moving air governing elimination. Its compression of the abdomen is the classical remedy for the bloating and constipation of aggravated Vata, and it is among the most reliably Vata-pacifying postures in the repertoire.

primary_benefits: Stretches the hamstrings and inner thighs of the lifted leg
Improves lateral pelvic stability and hip alignment
Strengthens the deep obliques that resist rotation
Opens the side body and improves overall balance
instructions: Lie on the right side with the body in one long line, right arm extended along the floor overhead.
Bend the right elbow and rest the head in the right hand, elbow grounded for stability.
Bend the left knee and catch the left big toe with the first two fingers and thumb of the left hand.
Exhale and extend the left leg straight up toward the ceiling, keeping both hips stacked vertically.
Resist the tendency to roll backward — the top hip must stay directly over the bottom hip.
Hold for 5 to 8 breaths, release, and roll over to repeat on the second side.
pranayama_sync: Exhale to extend the leg. Keep the breath even to hold the balance.
ayurvedic_rationale: Anantasana is named for Vishnu reclining on the serpent Ananta on the cosmic ocean — a posture of rest that nonetheless demands alertness. The side-lying position is grounding for Vata while the hamstring work maintains circulation. The pose teaches sthira sukham: steadiness within ease.

primary_benefits: Supports digestion and relieves gas buildup
Gently decompresses the lower back
Massages the abdominal organs
Helps release tension in the hips and sacrum
instructions: Lie on your back with both legs extended and arms resting by your sides.
Exhale and draw one knee toward your chest, then bring the other knee in.
Wrap your arms around the shins or knees without forcing the legs closer.
Keep the sacrum heavy and the shoulders relaxed on the floor.
If comfortable, lift the head slightly toward the knees without straining the neck.
Hold with smooth breathing, then release the legs back to the floor slowly.
pranayama_sync: Exhale as you draw the knees in to encourage release, and inhale softly into the back body while maintaining ease.
ayurvedic_rationale: Pavanamuktasana is a classic vata-pacifying pose because it supports downward-moving apana vayu and eases abdominal tension. It is often used to reduce bloating, calm the nervous system, and restore digestive comfort.

primary_benefits: Extreme opening of the hips, hamstrings, and groin
Deep spinal flexion and lengthening of the entire back body
Strong pratyahara — sensory withdrawal in a fully enclosed shape
Compresses and stimulates the abdominal organs
instructions: Lie supine and draw both knees toward the chest, warming the hips thoroughly first.
Take hold of the right foot with both hands and work the right leg behind the right shoulder.
Ease the leg further until the right ankle can rest behind the neck rather than on it.
Repeat with the left leg, crossing the left ankle over the right behind the head.
Bring the palms together at the heart and settle the shoulders down away from the ears.
Hold only while the breath stays completely free. Unhook the legs one at a time and rest in Savasana.
pranayama_sync: The breath must stay completely free. Any constriction of the throat or ribs means come out.
ayurvedic_rationale: Yoganidrasana is the yogic sleep posture, classically described as inducing a state between waking and sleeping. It is an advanced posture requiring years of hip preparation and, in an unsupervised setting, should be treated as aspirational. Any restriction of the breath means the pose is not yet available.

primary_benefits: Strengthens the legs, glutes, and core
Improves spinal rotation and thoracic mobility
Builds balance and concentration
Stimulates circulation and digestive fire
instructions: Stand with feet together or hip-width apart and bend the knees as if sitting back into a chair.
Bring the palms together at the heart and lengthen the spine on an inhale.
Exhale to rotate the torso to one side, bringing the opposite elbow toward the outer thigh if available.
If binding, wrap one arm behind the back and the other around the front only if the shoulders allow.
Keep the knees aligned and weight in the heels as you maintain the squat.
Lift the chest away from the thighs while continuing to breathe steadily.
Unwind slowly to center and repeat on the other side.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lift and lengthen, and exhale to deepen the twist while keeping the breath smooth and unforced.
ayurvedic_rationale: This strong twisting squat is heating and activating, making it useful for stimulating sluggish kapha and building digestive fire. Because it is more demanding, it should be used judiciously when pitta is already elevated.

primary_benefits: Improves spinal rotation and segmental mobility
Compresses and then flushes the liver, kidneys, and digestive organs
Stretches the outer hip, glutes, and shoulders
Relieves mid-back stiffness from prolonged sitting
instructions: Sit in Dandasana, then bend the right knee and place the right foot outside the left thigh.
Bend the left knee and tuck the left foot beside the right hip, or keep the left leg extended for a simpler version.
Sit on a folded blanket so both sitting bones stay grounded and the pelvis stays level.
Inhale and lengthen the spine, placing the right hand on the floor behind the sacrum as a light support, not a lever.
Exhale and rotate to the right, hooking the left elbow outside the right knee.
Turn the head last and least. Unwind on an exhale and repeat on the second side.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lengthen the spine, exhale to rotate deeper. Never twist on an inhale.
ayurvedic_rationale: Ardha Matsyendrasana is named for the sage Matsyendranath, a founding figure of Hatha Yoga. The wringing action on the abdominal organs is the classical method for kindling Agni and clearing Ama, making it especially valuable for manda (sluggish) digestion. Always lengthen before rotating — twisting a compressed spine is what injures discs.

primary_benefits: Detoxifies and wrings the torso through deep twisting
Improves ankle, knee, and hip mobility
Strengthens the feet, legs, and core
Supports digestion and spinal rotation
instructions: Begin in a squat with the feet together or nearly together.
Bring the torso forward between the thighs and lengthen the spine.
Hook one arm around both shins or wrap the arms around the legs if possible.
Rotate the chest and shoulders as much as comfortable without collapsing the spine.
Keep the heels grounded if possible and the knees tracking safely.
Breathe steadily, then unwind and repeat to the other side if practicing a variation.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lengthen the spine and exhale to deepen the twist, keeping the breath even and spacious.
ayurvedic_rationale: Pashasana is traditionally used to kindle digestive fire and mobilize stagnant energy in the lower body and torso. Its compressive twist can reduce Kapha heaviness and support Vata by improving circulation when practiced with stability.

primary_benefits: Deeply opens the side body, intercostals, and lats
Combines a lateral bend with a spinal twist for full ribcage mobility
Stretches the hamstring and inner thigh of the extended leg
Expands breathing capacity by mobilising the ribs
instructions: Sit with the right leg extended to the side and the left knee bent, left heel drawn toward the groin.
Sit on a folded blanket to keep the pelvis upright.
Rest the right forearm inside the right leg, palm facing up, and slide it toward the right foot.
Inhale and sweep the left arm overhead, rotating the chest open toward the ceiling.
Reach the left hand toward the right foot, keeping the left shoulder rolling back rather than collapsing forward.
Gaze up under the left arm if the neck allows. Hold for 5 to 8 breaths and change sides.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lengthen the side body, exhale to rotate the chest open.
ayurvedic_rationale: Parivrtta Janu Sirsasana opens the intercostals and the side body, directly expanding the field of Prana Vayu in the chest. The combined lateral bend and rotation is cooling and lengthening, making it well suited to Pitta, while the seated base keeps it grounding for Vata.

primary_benefits: Improves spinal rotation and mobility
Stretches hamstrings, hips, and shoulders
Builds balance and leg strength
Stimulates digestion and energizes the body
instructions: Begin in a standing lunge or triangle setup with one foot forward and the back foot turned slightly inward.
Square the hips as much as possible and lengthen the spine on an inhale.
Place the opposite hand on a block or the floor beside the front foot.
Exhale to rotate the torso, stacking the shoulders as you extend the other arm upward.
Keep both legs engaged and the front knee softly unlocked if needed.
Gaze upward or forward without straining the neck.
Hold with steady breaths, then unwind carefully and repeat on the other side.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lengthen the spine, and exhale to deepen the twist from the ribs and waist rather than forcing the neck.
ayurvedic_rationale: Twisting poses are traditionally used to kindle agni and support digestive flow, which can help reduce kapha stagnation. When practiced with moderation, this pose also creates clarity and openness without overly heating pitta.

primary_benefits: Stretches the hamstrings and inner thighs
Improves spinal rotation and upper-back mobility
Calms the nervous system while increasing circulation
Builds stability in the legs and core
instructions: Stand with the feet wide apart and place the hands on the hips.
Inhale to lengthen the spine and lift the chest.
Exhale to hinge forward from the hips until the torso is parallel or lower.
Place one hand on the floor or a block and rotate the torso, reaching the other arm upward.
Keep both legs active and distribute weight evenly through the feet.
Lengthen through the crown of the head while maintaining a steady twist.
Repeat on the other side after returning to center slowly.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to create space through the spine, and exhale to fold and rotate with control.
ayurvedic_rationale: This pose combines grounding forward flexion with a cleansing twist, which can help move stagnation and support healthy circulation. It is often used to balance kapha while maintaining enough steadiness to avoid aggravating vata.

primary_benefits: Improves spinal rotation with a strongly grounded base
Massages the abdominal organs and supports digestion
Stretches the shoulders and the outer hip
Builds the shoulder mobility that makes binds accessible
instructions: Sit in Dandasana, then bend the right knee and place the right foot flat on the floor close to the right sitting bone.
Keep the left leg extended and strongly active, foot flexed and thigh rooting down.
Inhale and lengthen the spine, lifting the crown.
Exhale and rotate to the right, hooking the left upper arm outside the right shin.
Place the right hand on the floor behind you and press down to lift and rotate further, or bind the hands behind the back if available.
Keep both sitting bones grounded. Release on an exhale and repeat on the second side.
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lengthen, exhale to twist. The rotation follows the exhale, never precedes it.
ayurvedic_rationale: Marichyasana is named for the sage Marichi, son of Brahma. The deep abdominal compression kindles Agni and assists elimination, and the pose is classically prescribed for sluggish digestion. The extended leg must stay active — a passive leg lets the twist migrate into the lumbar spine, which is where twisting injuries occur.

primary_benefits: Frees the shoulder joint through its full range without loading it
Relieves the upper-back and shoulder stiffness of desk work
Warms the rotator cuff before any weight-bearing pose
Improves circulation to the neck, shoulders and upper back
instructions: Sit in any comfortable cross-legged position or on a chair with the spine upright
Place the fingertips of each hand on the same-side shoulder, elbows out to the sides
Draw both elbows forward until they meet in front of the chest
Lift them upward towards the ears, then take them out and back, squeezing the shoulder blades
Lower them to the starting position to complete one slow circle
Continue for half the time in this direction, then reverse
Keep the head still and the breath even — the movement belongs to the shoulders alone
pranayama_sync: Inhale as the elbows lift and open, exhale as they close and lower
ayurvedic_rationale: Skandha Chakra belongs to the Pawanmuktasana series, whose purpose is to release trapped Vata from the joints before any stronger practice asks them to bear load. The shoulders are where Vata accumulates in anyone who sits and works with their hands, and stiffness there is Vata's dryness in the joint capsule. Rotating the joint through its own range, without weight on it, is the classical answer — movement and warmth rather than stretch.

primary_benefits: Mobilises the ankle joint and relieves stiffness from long sitting or standing
Improves venous return from the feet and lower legs
Prepares the ankles for standing balance work
Accessible from a chair, requiring no weight on the joint
instructions: Sit with the legs extended, hands behind for support, or upright on a chair
Keep the heels resting and the legs still
Rotate one foot slowly from the ankle, drawing the largest circle the joint allows
Complete slow circles in one direction, then reverse the same number
Change to the other foot, matching the count
Move from the ankle only — the knee and hip stay quiet
pranayama_sync: Breathe normally and slowly; let the circle take one full breath
ayurvedic_rationale: The feet are the seat of Apana Vata, and its downward flow stagnates first in the ankles — which is why swelling and stiffness there is the earliest sign of Vata obstruction in the lower body. The Pawanmuktasana joint practices treat exactly this, and they are prescribed for the elderly and the convalescent precisely because they ask nothing of strength or balance.

primary_benefits: Opens the side body and the space between the ribs
Tones the waist and the oblique muscles
Increases lateral flexibility of the spine, a direction most sequences neglect
Encourages fuller breathing by expanding the rib cage sideways
instructions: Stand with the feet hip-width apart and the weight even through both soles
Inhale and raise the right arm out to the side and up beside the ear, palm facing left
Exhale and bend directly to the left from the waist, letting the left hand slide down the left thigh
Keep both feet flat and the hips level — the bend belongs to the spine, not the pelvis
Do not lean forward or twist; the chest stays facing straight ahead
Hold with steady breath, then inhale to return upright and lower the arm
Repeat on the second side for the same length of time
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lengthen upward, exhale to bend sideways
ayurvedic_rationale: Lateral bending opens the flanks, where Kapha settles as heaviness and where the breath stops reaching in anyone who habitually breathes shallowly. It is the one spinal direction a standing sequence usually misses — forward, back and twist are everywhere, sideways is rare — so the side body stays short and the lower ribs stay closed. Both feet remain planted, so nothing is asked of balance.

primary_benefits: Loosens the waist, back and hips through gentle rhythmic rotation
Relieves the stiffness of prolonged sitting
Encourages peristalsis and eases sluggish digestion
Warms the spine for rotation without holding it under load
instructions: Stand with the feet about shoulder-width apart, arms relaxed at the sides
Keep the feet planted and the knees soft throughout
Swing both arms loosely to the right, letting the right arm wrap the waist and the left hand reach the right shoulder
Let the head turn with the shoulders and look over the right shoulder
Swing back through centre and repeat to the left — one swing each way is one round
Keep the movement loose and rhythmic rather than forced, and let the hips stay facing forward
Slow to a stop and stand still for a few breaths before the next pose
pranayama_sync: Exhale as you swing to each side, inhale through centre
ayurvedic_rationale: Kati Chakrasana is loosening rather than stretching — the rhythmic swing warms the lumbar region and moves Samana Vata through the abdomen, which is why it is traditionally practised before breakfast for sluggish digestion. Because nothing is held, it suits stiff and older practitioners who cannot yet sustain a seated twist, and it prepares the spine for the ones that are held later in the session.

primary_benefits: Mobilises the hip joint through its full circle without bearing weight
Strengthens the lower abdomen and the hip flexors gradually
Loosens the lower back from a fully supported position
Useful where standing work is not yet safe
instructions: Lie on the back with the legs together and the arms beside the body, palms down
Keep the head, shoulders and the opposite leg resting on the floor throughout
Raise the right leg a few inches, keeping the knee straight but not locked
Draw a slow circle with the whole leg from the hip, as large as the joint allows without the pelvis rolling
Complete the circles in one direction, then reverse
Lower the leg with control and rest a breath before changing sides
If the lower back lifts or aches, make the circle smaller — the pelvis staying still is the point
pranayama_sync: Breathe evenly throughout; never hold the breath while the leg is raised
ayurvedic_rationale: The hip is the largest joint Apana Vata governs, and the supine position lets it be moved through a full circle while the spine stays entirely supported. This is the classical progression for anyone whose back will not yet tolerate standing work: the same joint freedom, none of the load. Keep the far leg heavy on the floor — it is what stops the lumbar spine from taking the movement.

primary_benefits: Rotates the spine safely without the deep bind of the fuller twist
Massages the abdominal organs and supports digestion
Relieves stiffness across the middle and upper back
Opens the chest and encourages upright sitting posture
instructions: Sit with both legs extended forward and the spine upright
Bend the right knee and place the right foot flat on the floor beside the left knee
Place the right hand on the floor behind the sacrum, fingers pointing away
Bring the left hand to the outside of the right knee, or hug the knee if that is easier
Inhale to lengthen the spine upward, exhale to turn the chest to the right
Turn the head last and only as far as the neck allows comfortably
Release on an exhale, return to centre and repeat on the second side
Keep both sitting bones on the floor — lift one and the twist has become a lean
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lengthen the spine, exhale to turn a little further
ayurvedic_rationale: Vakrasana is the classical step before Ardha Matsyendrasana: the same rotation of the spine and the same compression of the abdominal organs that kindles Agni, but with the legs simple and no bind to force the twist deeper than the spine is ready for. Twisting moves Samana Vata through the digestive seat, which is why it is prescribed for sluggish digestion and abdominal heaviness.

primary_benefits: Tones the abdominal muscles and the waist through continuous movement
Massages the pelvic and abdominal organs
Loosens the lower back and hips from a seated position
Builds abdominal strength without any weight on the wrists
instructions: Sit with the legs extended and spread comfortably apart
Interlock the fingers and extend both arms forward at shoulder height
Keeping the elbows straight and the arms level, lean forward and sweep the hands out over the left leg
Continue the circle across towards the right leg, then lean back as the hands come towards the body
Move as though turning a heavy grinding wheel — large, slow and continuous
Complete the rounds in one direction, then reverse for the same count
Keep the knees straight but soft and the movement in the waist rather than the arms
pranayama_sync: Inhale as you lean back, exhale as you sweep forward
ayurvedic_rationale: Chakki Chalanasana takes its name and its shape from the hand mill, and the churning is literal: the whole abdomen is worked through a continuous circle rather than a held contraction. It is classically given for the pelvic organs and for Apana Vata's downward flow, and it builds abdominal strength for practitioners whose wrists cannot yet take plank or table work.

primary_benefits: Strengthens the lower back, glutes and hamstrings one side at a time
Builds spinal extension without the effort of lifting both legs
Tones the pelvic organs and supports elimination
Counteracts the forward-rounded posture of sitting
instructions: Lie face down with the chin resting on the floor and the legs together
Place the arms beneath the body, palms down under the thighs, or alongside the body
Inhale and raise the right leg as high as it will go without strain
Keep the knee straight, the hip bones level and the chin on the floor
Hold with normal breathing, then lower the leg slowly on an exhale
Rest for a breath, then repeat with the left leg for the same length
Do not let the raised hip lift or the body twist — height is not the point
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lift the leg, breathe normally in the hold, exhale to lower
ayurvedic_rationale: Ardha Salabhasana is the beginner's entry to the locust: one leg at a time asks roughly half the effort and lets the pelvis stay square, which is what makes the full pose unsafe for most new practitioners. The backward extension is warming and Kapha-reducing, and the pressure of the abdomen against the floor stimulates Agni and the pelvic organs.

primary_benefits: Opens the chest and the front of the shoulders
Releases tension across the upper back and between the shoulder blades
Stretches the shoulder joint in a direction daily life never uses
Improves the posture of anyone who works with their arms in front of them
instructions: Stand with the feet hip-width apart and interlock the fingers behind the back
Straighten the elbows and draw the shoulder blades towards each other
Inhale and lengthen the spine upward
Exhale and hinge forward from the hips only as far as the back stays straight, raising the clasped hands away from the back
Stop when the torso is around forty-five degrees — this is not a full forward fold
Keep the neck in line with the spine and the gaze forward and down
Inhale to rise, then release the hands and let the arms hang
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lengthen, exhale to hinge and lift the arms
ayurvedic_rationale: The chest is the seat of Prana Vata, and it closes in anyone who spends the day reaching forward — over a desk, a wheel or a child. Dwikonasana opens exactly that closure by taking the arms behind, a direction no ordinary movement uses, and the partial hinge keeps the head above the heart so it stays available to practitioners for whom a full forward fold is not.

primary_benefits: Opens the chest, throat and the front of the hips
Strengthens the muscles of the back through gentle extension
Improves breathing capacity by opening the front of the rib cage
Gives the benefit of the camel without reaching for the heels
instructions: Kneel with the knees hip-width apart and the shins flat, hips stacked over the knees
Place both palms on the back of the pelvis, fingers pointing down, elbows drawing together
Inhale and lift the chest upward, lengthening the whole spine before bending it
Exhale and ease the chest back and up, pressing the hips gently forward over the knees
Keep the head in line with the spine — do not drop it back
Support the lower back with the hands throughout and breathe steadily
Come up on an inhale, leading with the chest, and sit back on the heels to rest
pranayama_sync: Inhale to lift the chest, exhale to ease back; never hold the breath
ayurvedic_rationale: Backbending is the strongest Kapha-reducing direction, and it is also where a new practitioner most often hurts themselves by reaching for the heels before the spine can extend. Keeping the hands on the pelvis makes the lower back supported rather than hinged, so the opening happens at the chest where it is wanted. The throat opening is classically associated with clarity of expression.

primary_benefits: Releases tension held in the jaw, throat and face
Exercises the muscles of the face and the vocal apparatus
Relieves the held tightness that accompanies stress and suppressed speech
Requires no strength, balance or flexibility of any kind
instructions: Kneel and sit back on the heels, or sit upright on a chair with the feet flat
Place the palms on the knees with the fingers spread wide
Inhale deeply through the nose
Open the mouth wide, extend the tongue down towards the chin and exhale forcefully with an audible 'haa'
Widen the eyes and gaze at the point between the eyebrows or at the tip of the nose
Close the mouth, relax the face completely and breathe normally
Repeat several rounds, resting the face fully between each
pranayama_sync: A full inhale through the nose, a forceful audible exhale through the mouth
ayurvedic_rationale: Simhasana works on the throat, which Ayurveda treats as a seat of Udana Vata — the upward-moving breath that governs speech and expression. Tension there is held rather than felt, and the roar is the classical release for it. The pose asks nothing physical at all, which makes it one of the few genuinely available to every practitioner regardless of strength, stiffness or age.

primary_benefits: Strengthens the abdominal muscles and the hip flexors safely
Stretches the hamstring of the raised leg
Builds the core stability that protects the lower back
One leg at a time keeps the lumbar spine supported throughout
instructions: Lie on the back with the legs together and the palms flat beside the body
Press the lower back gently towards the floor and keep it there
Inhale and raise the right leg slowly to about ninety degrees, keeping the knee straight
Keep the left leg heavy on the floor, the foot relaxed
Hold with normal breathing, then exhale and lower the leg slowly without letting it drop
Rest a breath and repeat with the left leg
If the lower back arches away from the floor, bend the resting knee and place that foot down
pranayama_sync: Inhale to raise the leg, breathe normally in the hold, exhale to lower
ayurvedic_rationale: The single leg raise is the classical first step of the Pawanmuktasana strengthening group, and it is deliberately half of the double raise: with one leg still resting, the pelvis stays anchored and the lumbar spine is never asked to hold the load. That makes it one of the few abdominal practices appropriate for a back that is still recovering, and it kindles Agni through the same steady abdominal engagement.

primary_benefits: Relaxes the whole body while releasing the lower back
Encourages the natural curve of the lumbar spine to restore itself
Makes the diaphragm's movement obvious, since the abdomen presses the floor with each breath
The classical resting pose for anyone whose back is uncomfortable lying face up
instructions: Lie face down with the legs comfortably apart and the toes turned outward
Fold the arms in front of the body and rest the forehead on the crossed forearms
Raise the shoulders and head just enough that the chest is lifted slightly clear of the floor
Let the whole body soften and the belly rest heavily into the floor
Breathe naturally and feel the abdomen press down on each inhale
Stay still for the full time, letting each exhale release the lower back a little more
pranayama_sync: Natural abdominal breathing; do not shape the breath at all
ayurvedic_rationale: Makarasana is the prone counterpart to Savasana, and it is the resting pose given to practitioners with lower-back complaints for whom lying face up is uncomfortable — the position lets the lumbar curve settle rather than flatten. It is deeply Vata-pacifying: the ground contact across the whole front of the body is the grounding that restless, dry, mobile Vata most needs.
